headings.title: Definition and Overview of Gishiri Cut
headings.content: Gishiri cut is a traditional surgical practice performed predominantly in northern Nigeria and some other parts of West Africa. The term 'gishiri' is the Hausa word for salt, reflecting the historical practice of applying salt and local concoctions to the wound after the incision is made. This harmful traditional practice involves making a cut or incision inside the vagina using an unsterilized blade, razor, or sharp knife. Traditional birth attendants or local healers usually perform the procedure to treat a variety of perceived gynecological and obstetric conditions, ranging from prolonged labor and infertility to dysmenorrhea and low back pain. Despite aggressive public health campaigns and legislation against harmful traditional practices, gishiri cut remains a significant public health concern contributing to maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality in Nigeria. As nursing students, understanding this phenomenon is crucial for effective patient care, cultural sensitivity, and advocacy within Nigerian healthcare settings. Nurses must recognize that patients undergoing this practice often do so out of deeply ingrained cultural beliefs, necessitating education that is respectful yet firm regarding the associated health hazards.

headings.title: Cultural and Societal Context in Nigeria
headings.content: The practice of gishiri cut is deeply rooted in the cultural, social, and patriarchal context of certain communities in Nigeria. Traditional beliefs often attribute unexplained obstetric difficulties, infant illnesses, and gynecological disorders to supernatural causes or physical malformations within the female reproductive tract that require mechanical intervention. In many rural settings, traditional practitioners hold positions of high respect and authority, making their advice heavily influential over modern medical options. Socio-economic factors, such as poverty, lack of formal education, and poor geographical access to accredited healthcare facilities, further drive individuals toward traditional remedies. Gender inequality also plays a role, as women may lack the autonomy to make decisions regarding their own reproductive health and childbirth choices. Understanding these underlying societal pressures is vital for Nigerian nurses. Rather than stigmatizing patients who have experienced a gishiri cut, healthcare providers must adopt a holistic, empathetic approach that addresses the root cultural drivers while offering compassionate clinical care and community education.

headings.title: Indications According to Traditional Practitioners
headings.content: Traditional practitioners cite various indications for performing a gishiri cut, all of which stem from misconceptions about female anatomy and physiology. One of the most common purported indications is prolonged or obstructed labor, where practitioners believe the incision widens the birth canal to ease delivery. Other reported indications include primary or secondary infertility, painful menstruation (dysmenorrhea), frequent urination, vaginal discharge, and lower abdominal pain. In neonates, the cut may sometimes be performed in the mouth or perineal region to treat conditions like thrush or diarrhea. Practitioners believe that these ailments are caused by an internal swelling or blockage that can only be relieved by cutting the tissue. However, medical science clearly refutes these indications, demonstrating that the symptoms are either unrelated or actually exacerbated by the trauma of the procedure. For nursing students, recognizing these traditional beliefs helps bridge the communication gap between Western medical science and community health beliefs during patient counseling.

headings.title: Anatomical Structures Affected
headings.content: The anatomical structures affected by a gishiri cut depend on the site and depth of the incision, which is typically made blindly using crude instruments. Most commonly, the anterior or lateral walls of the vagina are slashed, which can easily extend into neighboring delicate organs. Because of the close anatomical proximity, the bladder and the urethra are frequently lacerated, leading to vesicovaginal fistulas (VVF) or urethrovaginal fistulas. In severe cases, deep lacerations can extend posteriorly toward the rectum, causing rectovaginal fistulas, or superiorly into the peritoneal cavity, resulting in severe internal hemorrhage. The extensive damage to the mucosal lining and underlying muscular layers of the vagina also leads to severe scarring, fibrosis, and anatomical distortion. This destruction compromises normal pelvic floor integrity and can cause long-term structural weakness. Student nurses must review pelvic anatomy thoroughly to understand how a single blade cut in the vaginal vault can disrupt multiple interconnected urogenital systems.

headings.title: Immediate and Long-Term Complications
headings.content: The complications of a gishiri cut are severe, debilitating, and can be life-threatening. Immediate complications include excruciating pain, severe primary hemorrhage, shock due to blood loss, and acute bacterial infections, including tetanus and sepsis from unsterilized instruments. Localized tissue trauma can also cause severe pelvic hematomas and swelling. Long-term complications are often devastating for the survivor's physical and psychosocial well-being. The formation of vesicovaginal or rectovaginal fistulas results in continuous, uncontrollable leakage of urine or feces, leading to chronic skin excoriation, malodor, and recurrent urinary tract infections. Furthermore, extensive vaginal scarring and fibrosis can cause dyspareunia (painful intercourse), complete vaginal stenosis, secondary infertility, and severe psychological trauma, including depression, anxiety, and social stigmatization. Recognizing these complications enables nurses to provide comprehensive rehabilitative care, addressing both the physical wounds and the profound emotional distress experienced by affected women.

headings.title: Clinical Assessment and Diagnosis in Nursing
headings.content: Clinical assessment and diagnosis of a gishiri cut require a high index of suspicion, sensitive communication, and a thorough physical examination by skilled healthcare professionals. When taking a patient history, nurses must inquire delicately about previous obstetric events, traditional interventions, or recent treatments for gynecological complaints. A thorough physical and speculum or bimanual pelvic examination allows the nurse and clinician to inspect the vaginal vault for lacerations, active bleeding, foreign substances (such as salt or herbs), and scar tissue. Assessment must also focus on identifying signs of infection, such as fever, foul-smelling discharge, or pelvic tenderness, as well as signs of hypovolemic shock from blood loss. In cases of suspected fistulas, specific diagnostic tests like the methylene blue test or cystoscopy may be performed. Nurses play a crucial role in preparing the patient for these examinations, ensuring privacy, offering emotional reassurance, and documenting findings accurately to guide prompt medical interventions.

headings.title: Medical and Surgical Management
headings.content: Medical and surgical management of complications arising from a gishiri cut requires a multi-disciplinary approach focused on stabilization and anatomical repair. Initial medical management prioritizes treating acute life threats: controlling hemorrhage with hemostatic agents or packing, fluid resuscitation for shock, administering broad-spectrum antibiotics to combat infection, and ensuring tetanus prophylaxis. Once the patient is stabilized and acute inflammation subsides, surgical intervention is often necessary. Surgical management includes wound debridement, primary repair of fresh lacerations, and specialized reconstructive surgery for established fistulas or severe vaginal stenosis. Post-operative nursing care is intensive, requiring careful monitoring of urinary catheter drainage, strict intake and output charting, pain management, and wound site hygiene to promote optimal healing and prevent graft or repair failure. Nurses must also coordinate closely with surgeons, physiotherapists, and mental health counselors to support complete recovery.

headings.title: Prevention, Advocacy, and Nursing Interventions
headings.content: Prevention, advocacy, and community-focused nursing interventions are vital in eradicating the harmful practice of the gishiri cut. Nurses serve as frontline educators and health advocates in primary healthcare centers and rural communities in Nigeria. Prevention strategies involve conducting community health outreach programs to educate traditional birth attendants, religious leaders, women's groups, and families about the dangers of harmful traditional practices and the benefits of skilled obstetric care. Advocacy efforts must also push for policies and community-based support systems that improve girl-child education, empower women economically, and increase healthcare accessibility. Furthermore, nurses must provide compassionate, non-judgmental support to survivors, helping them navigate social reintegration and mental health services. By combining clinical competence with active community engagement, nursing professionals can help protect vulnerable women and eliminate preventable maternal morbidity and mortality linked to gishiri cut.
